finding.new: Non-discriminating: the Chapman Sq ionospheric mechanism (Chapman 1919 and, for eclipses specifically, 1933; Yamazaki & Maute 2017; Kim & Chang 2018) predicts eclipse magnetic dips without dome geometry. The dome's station-to-station factor (FSF) follows from its flat Polaris-triangulation equation and equals the ratio of tan(latitude); its exponential height function plays no role. The absolute magnitude is imported from the 2017 Boulder observation, which the dome has since withdrawn as 'storm contamination' while still calibrating its 2026 predictions from it. GFZ Kp shows the 2017 eclipse ran at Kp 1+, not storm conditions.

detail_claim.new: Boulder (BOU) INTERMAGNET station observed a −10.9 nT anomaly at 17:20 UTC during the 2017 Aug 21 solar eclipse, described by the dome as coincident with eclipse maximum. (Boulder's eclipse maximum was at ≈17:46 UTC, about 26 minutes later.) The live dome site now cites the 2016-03-09 Pacific eclipse for WIN-010 instead.

detail_evidence.new:
Eclipse-induced magnetic perturbations follow from the Chapman Sq ionospheric framework: Chapman (1919, Phil. Trans. R. Soc. A 218:1–118) described the solar-driven daily variation, and Chapman (1933, “The effect of a solar eclipse on the Earth's magnetic field”, Terr. Magn. Atmos. Electr. 38:175–183) applied it to eclipses specifically. During an eclipse the Moon's shadow cuts ionizing UV, E-region conductivity falls, and the Sq current system weakens locally; the modern conductivity treatment is Yamazaki & Maute (2017, Space Science Reviews 206:299–405). Kim & Chang (2018, Advances in Space Research 61:2040–2049), analysing roughly 200 records from 100 INTERMAGNET observatories over 1991–2016, find the eclipse effect grows with eclipse magnitude and is most conspicuous at magnetic latitudes of 30°–50°. Boulder sits inside that band (≈48° by either the centered-dipole or AACGM convention) and saw about 93–94% obscuration under a near-midday Sun in 2017, so the Sq framework expects a depression of order 10 nT there. That is the size of the −10.9 nT value. We have not run a multi-station timing analysis of the 2017 event and do not claim one: the dome's minimum at 17:20 UTC sits about 26 minutes before Boulder's eclipse maximum (≈17:46 UTC; timeanddate.com local circumstances, magnitude 0.940; DE421 ephemeris gives 17:47 UTC and 93.6%), and the dome's own later audit says its 2017 minima did not track eclipse timing (see below). The dome has no equation that derives eclipse magnitudes from dome parameters; it observes the signal and counts it as a WIN.

Kp record (corrected 2026-09-27). Earlier versions of this entry said the 2017 observation “was recorded at Kp ≈ 3” and called 2016-03-09 “a genuinely Kp<2 quiet day.” Both statements were wrong, and we are correcting them against the same source we use to audit the dome in WIN-025: the GFZ Potsdam definitive Kp record (kp.gfz.de; responses archived in data/dome-api-snapshots/gfz-kp-eclipse-windows-2026-09-27.json). For the 3-hour slot containing each eclipse: 2016-03-09 (Guam eclipse 00:22–03:00 UTC, maximum 01:52): Kp 2o, which is at the dome's threshold rather than below it. 2017-08-21 (Boulder eclipse 16:24–19:14 UTC, maximum ≈17:46, dome minimum 17:20): Kp 1+ in the 15–18 UTC slot and 2o in the 18–21 UTC slot. The day's peak of Kp 3o fell at 06–09 UTC, about ten hours before the eclipse. 2024-04-08 (North American eclipse; see WIN-025): Kp 1+ at 15–18 UTC and 0+ at 18–21 UTC. None of the three days approached storm level (NOAA's G1 threshold is Kp 5). On the planetary index, the eclipse the dome calls “the quietest eclipse day on record” (2016) had the highest eclipse-slot Kp of the three, and the two it labels “storm-contaminated” (2017, 2024) were at Kp 1+ and 0+.

What the dome gets right here: its model page correctly notes that 2017-08-21 was “geomagnetically disturbed pre-eclipse” (the morning Kp 3o), and it ranks events by local Boulder variability (standard deviation 2.23 nT in 2016, 8.05 nT in 2017, 5.59 nT in 2024 per the live wins.html WIN-010 entry). Local variance is a reasonable detectability measure. Its labels, however, do not follow Kp, and the dome does not say over which window the variance was computed. If that window is the eclipse itself, the ranking is confounded by local time. The 2016 eclipse fell at 17:22–20:00 MST in Boulder, around dusk, when Sq variation is weak. The 2017 and 2024 eclipses both fell near Boulder's local noon, when Sq variation and any eclipse effect are largest. A midday eclipse raises Boulder's variance on its own; that is not storm contamination. (This local-time reading is our inference and has not been checked against the dome's unstated window.)

The dome's monitor.py carries a “Kp < 2 required for eclipse signal” label (domain #12), but it only logs the latest real-time NOAA Kp value; it does not gate or score any eclipse result. The Kp < 2 precondition lives on the dome's predictions page (“Eclipse predictions valid only if Kp < 2 on August 12, 2026”; Tier 3: “Kp < 2 entire Aug 9–12 window”). What happened when that condition was tested on 12 August 2026 is covered in the post-event status in the verdict text.

The station scaling (FSF). The dome's 2026 predictions multiply a baseline by each station's coverage and a “field strength factor” (FSF) it attributes to “V12 H(r)/r dome geometry.” Solving the dome's V12 equation r·tan(θ) = 8537·exp(−r/8619) for each station's latitude and normalizing to Boulder reproduces all nine published FSF values (0.642–2.075) to within 0.6% at seven stations and 2.78% at the worst (Pearson r = 0.9999). But V12 is r·tan(θ) = H(r) with θ set equal to geographic latitude, so H(r)/r = tan(latitude) at every station and FSFi = tan(lati)/tan(latBOU) exactly, whatever H(r) is. Pure tan(lat)/tan(40.015°) matches the published table at r = 0.999915, with seven of nine stations within 0.1%. The genuine dome content in the FSF is V12 itself, the flat-geometry Polaris triangulation. The exponential H(r) and its 8537/8619 km constants contribute nothing; the published table can be reproduced with a calculator from station latitudes alone.

The magnitude is imported, and the dome has disowned its source. The scaling does not supply the Boulder magnitude. The dome's 2026-03-12 table used the 2017 BOU value (−10.9 nT) as its baseline. Its model page later re-audited the same 2017 event at −18.22 nT against a 2017-08-20 quiet-day baseline (OPEN-009, model.html) and told readers to multiply every BOU-column prediction by 1.672 (= 18.22/10.9). Meanwhile PROS-003 on wins.html (status dated 2026-03-15) says: “Timing audit shows Z minima uncorrelated with eclipse geometry across 2017 and 2024 events (scatter −180 to +111 min from totality). Anomalies attributed to geomagnetic storm contamination, not eclipse signal.” The dome removed the 2017 event as evidence but kept it as the calibration for its only prospective eclipse prediction, as the numerator of WIN-012's coupling constant (monitor.py domain #7: kappa_obs = 10.9 / 6.5), and as the −18.22 nT baseline in its automated eclipse scoring (monitor.py domain #10).

Dome-side update (verified 2026-07-19, re-checked 2026-09-27). The live site now titles this entry “WIN-010 — Eclipse Magnetic Signal Confirmed on Quiet Days” and rests it on the 2016-03-09 Pacific total eclipse: GUA −13.16 nT (SNR 4.85), Z-component minima within 30 minutes of totality at five stations (GUA −3, HON +15, MMB +17, CNB −10, GNG +9 min) and H-component tracking at three (MMB −19, CNB +6, ASP −25 min). Multi-station timing coherence within about ±25 minutes of totality is real and worth having, and it is exactly what the Sq framework predicts for a sunlit ionosphere under the shadow. It does not discriminate between the dome and standard physics. The same holds for the confirmed nine-station 2024 cohort in WIN-025 (Chernogor & Holub, 2024). Verdict unchanged: Std Model Explains.

detail_verdict_text.new:
Non-discriminating. The Chapman Sq framework (Chapman 1919; Chapman 1933 for eclipses; Yamazaki & Maute 2017) predicts eclipse-correlated magnetic perturbations without any dome parameter, and Kim & Chang (2018, Adv. Space Res. 61:2040–2049) confirm statistically across INTERMAGNET that the effect scales with eclipse magnitude and is strongest at magnetic latitudes 30°–50°. The dome's own predictions page concedes the point. Its Tier 1 block is headed “Magnetic Signal (Globe-Compatible)” and gives the globe prediction as “0.0 nT systematic (or ionospheric Sq disruption — competing mechanism exists, see WIN-068 honest caveat)” (predictions.html), while its WIN-010 entry says “Globe has no mechanism predicting eclipse-correlated magnetic anomalies.” Those two dome pages contradict each other, and the first one agrees with this verdict.

The magnitude is borrowed, then reused. The dome's formula ΔZ = baseline × coverage × FSF takes its magnitude from observation. The 2017 Boulder value served as a confirmed WIN, as WIN-012's coupling-constant numerator (κ = 10.9/6.5), and as the 2026 baseline. Training data cannot also be test data. The 2026-03-12 table added a second anchor, the Mohe 1997 “W004 empirical” value of −22.24 nT (the event behind WIN-014, which our review rates Refuted by Data), giving two prediction columns about a factor of two apart at every station (10.9/22.24 = 0.490). Almost any post-eclipse value sits nearer one column than the other, which invites choosing the anchor after the fact. The dome has published at least five different Ebro figures for the same event: −10.7 nT (BOU column) and −21.7 nT (W004 column) on 2026-03-12; about −17.8 nT after the 2026-03-28 ×1.672 correction; “−17 to −21 nT at stations with >80% coverage” on the predictions page; and −28.9 nT in its automated scoring. The last comes from monitor.py computing −18.22 × 0.95 × 1.672. Since −18.22 = −10.9 × 1.672 already, the correction is applied twice and Ebro's FSF (1.029) is dropped. Kill Shots Test 5 tracks the same spread.

What we grant on the scaling. The FSF is dome geometry. It follows from V12, the flat Polaris triangulation r·tan(θ) = H(r), which makes FSF = tan(lat)/tan(latBOU). The part the dome presents as its derivation, the exponential H(r) with its 8537/8619 km constants, drops out and contributes nothing (details in the evidence panel; WIN-044 covers the dome's separate three-constant FSF(lat) fit). A correct ratio between stations still does not predict the signal. Section 1.8 (The Coordinate Collapse) adds that the disc radii feeding V12 come from Polaris elevations that pass through the same n(r) medium the dome says is 300–6,000× more refractive than Earth's atmosphere.

The Kp argument, corrected. An earlier version of this verdict argued that the dome accepted a Kp ≈ 3 observation as a WIN while demanding Kp < 2 for future tests. The GFZ definitive record does not support that. The 2017 eclipse ran at Kp 1+ (the Kp 3o came ten hours earlier), and the 2016 replacement ran at Kp 2o (figures and sources in the evidence panel). We withdraw the asymmetric-standard argument. The corrected record points to a stronger problem. The dome's quiet/storm split does not track Kp at all: the two eclipses it calls storm-contaminated (2017 at Kp 1+, 2024 at Kp 0+) were quieter on the planetary index than the one it calls the quietest on record (2016 at Kp 2o). Yet the dome withdrew the 2017 event on storm grounds (PROS-003, 2026-03-15) and kept it as the calibration for every 2026 prediction (OPEN-009 on model.html; monitor.py domains #7 and #10). Either the 2017 event is contaminated, in which case the dome's 2026 magnitudes and WIN-012's κ rest on a contaminated number, or it is sound, in which case the withdrawal was wrong. The dome cannot have both. This argument does not depend on any of our physics.

Post-hoc test. Independent of the physics, this claim fails our post-hoc test. The confirming values come from public INTERMAGNET archives that predate the dome's 2026 registrations (live WIN-010: “Registered: Originally 2026-03-06 | Audited: 2026-03-15”), and we found no pre-registration of the expected value in a timestamping venue independent of the author. Under the dome author's own definition (“prediction was timestamped before confirming data was pulled”), temporal ordering cannot be established from the repository history.

The 2026-08-12 test as we pre-registered it, and its limits. Before the eclipse we pre-registered a comparison of per-station residuals, (observed ΔZ) / (baseline × coverage), against two profiles: the dome's FSF (tan of geographic latitude) and a magnetic-latitude profile based on Kim & Chang's 30°–50° band. Stations inside the band were expected to carry an ensemble-median signal. Stations outside it were expected to fall to ≤30% of the in-band median, a first-order bound adopted because the paper does not tabulate the out-of-band drop-off. That gave a crude but falsifiable nine-number competitor to the dome's nine FSF numbers. We also pre-registered a coverage-exponent sensitivity check: divide observed ΔZ by baseline × coverageα for α ∈ {0.5, 0.8, 1.0, 1.2, 1.5}. If the ranking of the two profiles holds across that range, the linear-coverage approximation is adequate; if it flips, neither profile can claim the result. The frozen registration is predictions/eclipse-2026-08-12-predictions.json (OpenTimestamps-anchored 2026-05-02). The evaluation must report four limitations that were not handled in advance. We are stating them now, before any residuals are published. (1) Coverage inputs. The pre-registration did not say whose coverage values the residual uses. The dome's per-station “coverage” figures are far below ephemeris obscuration at the northern stations: Niemegk 40% vs about 85%, Lerwick 42% vs 88%, Eskdalemuir 55% vs 91%, Chambon 70% vs 93%, Hartland 80% vs 94% (JPL DE421 ephemeris; Hartland confirmed independently, see below). The ratio reaches about ×2.1 at Niemegk and Lerwick and correlates with FSF (r ≈ 0.84). A residual built on the dome's coverage would therefore inflate exactly where FSF predicts larger values. The evaluation will report both versions and label the ephemeris version as post-hoc. Separately, the dome's per-station predictions fail on geometry inputs alone, whatever the magnetometers show. (2) Solar elevation. The Sun stood only 3°–14° above the horizon at eclipse maximum at every European station, against 57° at Boulder in 2017. Sq conductivity is much weaker near sunset, so neither the dome's linear formula nor our daytime-derived ensemble comparator was scaled for this; our own amplitude range may be too high. (3) Coordinate label. The station magnetic latitudes we pre-registered (COI 43.7°, EBR 42.9°, SPT 42.4°, CLF 49.6°, Canary 33.2°, NGK 51.85°, HAD 53.6°, ESK 57.5°, LER 61.8°) are centered-dipole values (IGRF-14 epoch-2020 pole 80.65°N, 287.32°E), computed by us. Earlier text mislabelled them “CGM” and attributed them to an IAGA registry. Under the AACGM-v2 convention they are 4°–10° lower (EBR 33.3°, SPT 31.1°, COI 32.0°, CLF 42.8°, HAD 46.7°, NGK 47.9°, ESK 51.9°, LER 57.5°). Hartland and Niemegk would then move inside the band, and Kim & Chang's abstract does not state which convention their 30°–50° band uses. Only Lerwick and Eskdalemuir fall outside the band under both conventions, so the discriminating signal rests on fewer stations than we claimed. The dipole-latitude correlation with geographic latitude (r = 0.991 over the eight European stations) is higher still under AACGM (r = 0.999), which makes the overlap between the two profiles worse. (4) Station labels and availability. The Canary station, labelled “SNK” in the dome's table, is INTERMAGNET GUI (Güímar). The dome's own station audit flags Coimbra as having no data and Lerwick as having 2023 data only. Coimbra could not be retrieved from INTERMAGNET for the evaluation. Given these limits, an outcome in which FSF tracks the residuals better than magnetic latitude would not by itself be evidence for dome physics, because both confounds favour FSF. We withdraw our earlier statement that such an outcome would leave “something non-trivial” to explain.

Post-event status (dated 2026-09-27). The eclipse occurred on 12 August 2026. Conditions: GFZ definitive Kp for 9–12 August peaked at 3o (11 August, 15–18 UTC). On the eclipse day it was 1+ at 15–18 UTC and 2+ at 18–21 UTC, and the European partial phases (about 17:00–19:45 UTC) straddle both slots. The dome's precondition failed on both of its stated readings (“valid only if Kp < 2 on August 12”; “Kp < 2 entire Aug 9–12 window”). Its rule says “IF Kp ≥ 3 … not a falsification” and says nothing about 2 ≤ Kp < 3, which is where the eclipse slot fell. The escape clause this entry warned about has now fired. The dome's result: none posted, 46 days after the event and well past the dome's own “within 72h” and “within 24h” statements. None can be posted automatically: monitor.py domain #10 hardcodes observed = 'PENDING' and pass = None and has no code path that fetches INTERMAGNET data. The latest status_history.json record (2026-09-27T04:39Z) still reads PENDING at −47 days. Its stated falsification rule, “Fails if measured anomaly within ±3 nT of 0,” is one-sided: any |ΔB| above 3 nT counts as success. Our result: our own page set a +30-day evaluation date of about 11 September 2026, and we missed it. A draft evaluation was run on 26 September and is now in adversarial review. That review found it needs substantial revision, including scoring the dome's Z-component, contact-phase template on the dome's own terms. We are therefore not publishing magnetic verdicts here yet; the target for publishing the reviewed evaluation, with every registered claim scored, is 2026-10-15. Symmetry: our frozen standard-physics claim (B1-M-001) is also conditioned on Kp < 2 and treats Kp ≥ 2 as noise-inflating rather than falsifying. We cannot count the dome's Kp escape clause against it while relying on the same clause ourselves. What separates the two sides is that we will publish our scored result, including any misses. A miss we already know about: our frozen geometric claim B1-G-005 registered Hartland's maximum obscuration as 88% ± 2 percentage points. The true value is about 94%: 94.4% at 18:15 UTC from two independent DE421 computations, and magnitude 0.947 (≈94% obscuration) with the partial phase 17:17–19:08 UTC from timeanddate.com for Bideford, 18 km east of the observatory. That is about 4 percentage points outside our own bound. We record B1-G-005 as failed. The frozen file stays unedited; the correction goes in a dated erratum. Our §4.2.7 figures (≈88% peak, “roughly 2 h 45 min” partial phase; the true duration is ≈1 h 51 min) are corrected there. The error does not bear on the dome-versus-globe shadow-geometry verdict, which rests on the path and size of totality.

Note: WIN-010, WIN-025, and WIN-068 all rest on the same Sq mechanism. Count inflation does not by itself refute any individual claim, but it is relevant context when the dome cites 69 confirmed predictions: three of them share one mechanism.

tldr_evidence.new: Eclipses cause small magnetic dips because the Moon's shadow weakens the electric currents in the sunlit upper atmosphere, a mechanism Chapman worked out for eclipses in 1933. Boulder's −10.9 nT in 2017 is the size that mechanism predicts, so the agreement is expected rather than a dome discovery. The dome has since moved this WIN to a 2016 Pacific eclipse, and the same mechanism covers that event too.

tldr_verdict.new: Standard physics predicts this signal without dome parameters; the dome's station scaling is just the ratio of tan(latitude), and the signal's size is borrowed from the 2017 Boulder data. The dome now calls that 2017 event storm-contaminated (planetary Kp says it was quiet) yet still uses it to calibrate its 2026 predictions. On 12 August 2026 the dome's own Kp precondition failed and it has posted no result; our own magnetic evaluation is late and still under review.

kernel_of_truth: The dome is right that eclipses produce measurable ground magnetic perturbations, right that geomagnetic quietness matters for detecting them, right that 2017-08-21 was disturbed in the morning (Kp 3o at 06-09 UT), and local Boulder variance is a reasonable detectability heuristic. Its FSF table genuinely follows from its own V12 flat triangulation, and pre-committing station-level numbers before 2026-08-12 was the right methodological move. None of that makes the signal a dome prediction: the magnitude is borrowed from an event the dome itself now disowns, its quiet/storm labels run opposite to the planetary Kp record, its coverage inputs are wrong by up to ~x2 against ephemeris, and its own precondition failed on the day.

anticipated_objections.objection: "You got both Kp values backwards and attacked us for the same error in WIN-025."
anticipated_objections.response: Conceded and corrected in-text with a dated correction note, using the same GFZ source as WIN-025. The corrected record hurts the dome more: its "quietest day" (2016, Kp 2o) was noisier on Kp than both "storm" days (2017 Kp 1+, 2024 Kp 0+), and it disowned 2017 while keeping it as calibration.

anticipated_objections.objection: "Quietness should be judged by local BOU variance, not planetary Kp."
anticipated_objections.response: Granted as a heuristic in the text. But the dome itself states its precondition in Kp, and if its variance is taken over the eclipse window it is confounded by Boulder local time (2016 at dusk vs 2017/2024 near noon). The local-time reading is flagged as our inference, not a verified fact.

anticipated_objections.objection: "By our pre-registered rule 2026 is not a falsification (Kp ≥ 2), and your frozen file says the same."
anticipated_objections.response: Agreed and stated symmetrically in the post-event paragraph. The text does not score the dome's escape clause against it. It records that the clause fired, that the dome's rule is silent on 2 ≤ Kp < 3, and that the dome's code cannot post any result, whereas we commit to publishing ours with misses.
